CS166 Problem Set 5: Lensless Imaging

Instructions

  • This problem set is due on Tuesday, May 19th at 10AM.

  • Please abide by the collaboration policy on the Canvas page.

  • To hand in your work, upload a ZIP archive to Gradescope containing

    • a document called report.pdf with your name, your solutions, and the amount of time it took you to complete the assignment, and
    • the images used in your answers, named as specified by the questions.

  • The inputs and outputs to the provided Raspberry Pi scripts will be grayscale, demosaiced raw images, in “.npz” format.

  • The images you submit and include in your report will be gamma-encoded PNG rendings of these. When rendering, scale the dynamic range to amplify details while avoiding clipping.

  • If your problem set is too large for Gradescope, you can upload just your report, and submit your full solutions here.

Questions

  1. Building a lensless camera (25%): Take a picture of a scene with your PiCam using the capture-image script provided, invoked with --mode=gray. This script is a bit different than the version used in previous problem sets, so make sure to copy it over. Render this image as q1-lens.png and include it in your report.


    A schematic side view of the diffuser camera.

    Next, carefully unscrew the PiCam’s lens (the slightly darker circular insert into the larger gray lens holder) using a pair of tweezers or your fingers. Do not remove the tube in which it resides. Take a picture of the same scene, render it as q1-uncovered.png, and include it in your report.

    Then, place a piece of clear, double-sided tape over the lens holder, replacing the lens. Use strips of black tape to create an aperture. Use the capture-image script to visualize the point spread function (PSF) induced by a point source—e.g. a cell phone flashlight held 2 meters away—in a dark room (it is very important that the room be as dark as possible). Make sure the entire cropped PSF is within the sensor’s field of view, but occupies most of it.

    Take a third picture of the scene, render it as q1-diffuser.png, and include it in your report. Then take a picture of your modified PiCam, save it as q1-setup.png, and include that in your report.


    The PiCam converted to a diffuser camera.

  2. Capturing a dark frame and the point spread function (25%): Capture an image with the camera completely covered, to block out all light, render it as q2-dark-frame.png, and include it in your report. Next, capture an image of the same point source you used to size your aperture (your point spread function). Render this image as q2-psf.png and include it in your report. When capturing these images, you may adjust the capture-image parameters to achieve a higher signal-to-noise ratio. If you do so, however, make sure to use the same values for both images, and for the rest of the problem set.

  3. Deconvolving captured images (25%): Position your camera facing a computer screen. Map the camera’s field of view using your point light source. Project star.png on the screen such that the entire star is within the camera’s field of view. Make the screen as bright as possible. Capture an image, render it as q3-star-captured.png, and include it in your report. Then run the deconvolve script, render the result as q3-star-deconvolved.png, and include it in your report. Repeat this process projecting heart.png, to generate q3-heart-captured.png and q3-heart-deconvolved.png. Repeat this process again with a high-contrast scene, e.g. your hand, illuminated by a flashlight from below (while still keeping the room as dark as possible), to generate q3-scene.png, q3-scene-captured.png, and q3-scene-deconvolved.png.


    Left: A captured image. Right: The result of deconvolution.

  4. Reading and discussing a paper (25%): Summarize a conference or journal paper related to your final project. Google Scholar is a good place to start. Relevant publication venues include ICCP, ICCV, CVPR, ECCV, Siggraph, and Transactions on Computational Imaging. (2 paragraphs) Discuss the scientific contributions made by the paper, as you would if you were a peer reviewer. (1 paragraph) Additionally, discuss how you the paper (and the experiments behind it) might be improved. Keep in mind that even papers that make it through the peer review process may have some weaknesses, and questions the authors left unexplored. (1 paragraph)

Notes

  • The Scotch tape camera setup is based on a tutorial written by Camille Biscarrat and Shreyas Parthasarathy, in Prof. Laura Waller’s lab at UC Berkeley.
  • More information about the lab’s work with diffuser cameras can be found here.
